title: Water: the next source of conflict?
subtitle: The blue gold of the 21st century
subject: comprendreLeMonde
description: Less than 1% of the water on Earth is fresh and easy to reach. Some experts already see it as the next great source of conflict.

hero.hook: Less than 1% of the water on Earth is fresh and reachable. The rest is fought over.

blocks.text: Fresh water is the resource most essential to human life. It is also getting scarcer: the population is growing, the climate is shifting, and some experts already predict the first “water wars” of the 21st century.
This course explores why such a vital resource is becoming a major strategic issue, able to bring neighboring countries together, or to set them against each other.

Water covers 70% of the Earth, which earns it the nickname “blue planet.” But almost all of that water is salty. Fresh water is only about 3% of the total, and two thirds of it is locked up as ice in the polar caps and the glaciers. In the end, liquid fresh water we can actually reach (lakes, rivers, shallow water tables) is less than 1% of all the water on the planet.

blocks.caption: Accessible fresh water is less than 1% of all the water on Earth

blocks.text: This scarcity is not shared out evenly. Some countries, such as Brazil, Canada and Russia, hold immense reserves. Others, in the Middle East and North Africa, live with lasting **[[water stress]]**: their demand for water is greater than their territory can supply. In 2024, about 4 billion people spend at least one month a year in that situation.
In the 20th century the world population tripled, but water use was multiplied by six, driven above all by industrialization and by diets that contain far more meat.

Tension arises above all when a resource is shared. More than 260 rivers in the world are **transboundary**: they cross several countries, creating a forced dependence between the states upstream, which control the source, and those downstream, which take whatever is left.

The Nile shows this tension well. Ethiopia built the **[[GERD]]**, an immense dam on the Blue Nile, to produce electricity and become more self-sufficient. But Egypt, which depends on the Nile for 95% of its water, sees every cubic meter held back upstream as a direct threat to its security.
The Indus Waters Treaty, signed in 1960 between India and Pakistan, survived three wars between the two countries without ever being broken: proof that water can also be a powerful tool of peace.

Faced with shrinking supplies, some countries bet on technology. **Desalination**, which turns seawater into drinking water, has taken hold in the Gulf states and the Near East. Israel produces more than 80% of its drinking water in desalination plants. The process is still costly and energy-hungry, and it discharges **brine**, very salty water that can damage marine ecosystems.
Other solutions rely on restraint. Drip irrigation, which brings water straight to the roots of plants, cuts farm water use by 30% to 70%.
In **[[Singapore]]**, a tiny territory with no large water reserve, wastewater is treated so thoroughly that it comes out purer than spring water, then goes back into use under the name “NEWater.”

sections.title: Toward shared governance of blue gold

blocks.text: Despite the predictions of “water wars,” history shows that this resource has served cooperation more often than open conflict. Setting up river basin commissions and treaties between neighbors is still the best way to avoid a crisis.

One concept helps to grasp the scale of the problem: **[[virtual water]]**, the amount of water needed to make a product. When a country under water stress imports wheat, it is really importing the water used to grow it somewhere else. It takes about 15,000 liters of water to produce a single kilogram of beef, against 1,500 liters for a kilogram of wheat.

Accessible fresh water is less than 1% of the water on Earth, and hundreds of millions of people live in basins shared between countries with opposing interests. Technology and international cooperation remain the best weapons against the water crises to come.
